The right one: for an efficiently computable f, the sequence k -> f(x(kP)) has DFT over Z/n whose nonzero-frequency coefficients are all O(sqrt n) for RATIONAL f by Weil/Bombieri-type bounds - but no such bound directly covers functions of the INTEGER/BIT representation, where the special shape of p (2^256 = 2^32 + 977 mod p) couples high and low bits after reduction. If any bit-level f has a coefficient of magnitude >> sqrt(n) polylog, Goldreich-Levin / sparse-FFT recovery finds a frequency and with it exploitable structure.
nongeneric_structure: Two distinct hooks: (i) the integer/bit representation of F_p elements, which is not an algebraic function of the point and therefore outside the reach of the standard character-sum bounds; (ii) the pseudo-Mersenne shape of p, which makes 'top 32 bits' and 'low 32 bits' algebraically related through reduction. The measured object is a spectrum of a coordinate function, not an enumeration of group elements, so this is not a re-encoded generic search - and indeed a generic-group algorithm has no f to evaluate.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Bombieri 1966 'On exponential sums in finite fields' - square-root cancellation for character sums along curves. [ESTABLISHED, high confidence] Kohel & Shparlinski 2000 (ANTS-IV) 'Exponential sums and group generators for elliptic curves over finite fields'. SEARCH: 'Lange Shparlinski certain exponential sums random walks elliptic curves' - should give nontrivial bounds on sums of additive characters over multiples of a point, i.e. exactly flat spectra for algebraic f. [ESTABLISHED] Akavia, Goldwasser, Safra 2003 (FOCS) 'Proving hard-core predicates using list decoding' - the algorithmic tool for finding heavy Fourier coefficients of a function on Z_N with query access. [ESTABLISHED] Boneh & Venkatesan 1996 (CRYPTO) hidden number problem - proof that SOME bit-level structure is exploitable once partial information leaks. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: the published bounds cover rational f; here the search is explicitly over non-algebraic bit functions and includes a LEARNED f optimised to maximise a spectral peak, with a permutation null model to calibrate the Rayleigh baseline.
smallest_experiment: PILOT ALREADY RUN (script: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-virtualaquarium/e2bf485c-5536-57b5-8ef5-8e69bb3bcc7b/scratchpad/fourier.py). Full tables of x(kP), y(kP) for k = 1..n-1 on y^2=x^3+7 at 12/14/16/18 bits; for f in {lsb(x), 1[x < p/2], top-bit(x), QR(x), lsb(y)}, centred, numpy FFT over Z/n, statistic max_{c != 0}|F_f(c)|/sqrt(n). RESULT: 1.64, 1.84, 1.79, ~2.0, 1.56 at 12 bits; 1.68-2.09 at 14; 1.97-2.15 at 16; 2.04-2.22 at 18. max/mean ratio 4.1-5.5 throughout - exactly the Rayleigh maximum-of-n-Gaussians null, i.e. flat spectra, consistent with the Weil-type expectation. EXTENSION: (1) push to 2^22-2^24 (a 16M-point FFT is minutes; table generation with the repo's C group law); (2) widen the f family - single-bit extracts at every position, sliding windows, x mod small m, CRT combinations, interval indicators of varying width, and functions of (x,y) jointly; (3) LEARNED f: parameterise f as a small MLP/linear model over bit features, relax the peak statistic to a differentiable surrogate (max over a fixed candidate frequency set of |sum_k f_theta(x(kP)) e(ck/n)|) and gradient-ascend on theta; (4) null model: recompute the same statistic after randomly permuting the table, 100 replicates, to get the exact null band; (5) plot normalised peak vs log2 n for every f, and test for an upward trend.
kill_criteria: DEAD if for every f in the searched family (including the learned f) and every size up to 2^24, the normalised peak stays inside 1.3x the permutation-null band and shows no positive trend in log2 n. DEAD also if a heavy coefficient is found but does not reproduce on a different base point or a different curve of the same shape (a curve-specific artefact), or if it disappears when the learned f is retrained with the table split into train/test halves. The pilot has already passed the null band at 12-18 bits, so the surviving hope is only the special-p regime at large sizes, which the toy curves cannot fully imitate - state that limitation openly.
expected_complexity: If some f had a single coefficient of magnitude eps*n, sparse recovery (Akavia-Goldwasser-Safra / sparse FFT) finds the frequency in time poly(log n, 1/eps), which would be a polynomial-time distinguisher and, with a small amount of additional structure, a break. That requires eps >> 1/sqrt(n), i.e. a violation of square-root cancellation for a non-algebraic f - the precise thing that must be true. Nothing weaker than eps = n^(-1/4) would even be interesting, since rho already gives n^(1/2).
novelty_note: This replaces the straw-man 'measure mutual information between k and kP' (which is maximal by bijectivity and therefore uninformative) with a statistic that has a provable null for algebraic f and a genuine open corner for bit-level f, and it comes with a pilot that already demonstrates the null band. A positive result would be a clean, small, checkable finding rather than a vague 'the model learned something'.

title: Can a LEARNED advice string beat the generic ST^2 = Theta(n) preprocessing trade-off?
surface: 7d/7 general - ML as a lossy compressor of the group, measured against a tight generic lower bound
hypothesis: With S bits of preprocessing advice and T online group operations, generic algorithms satisfy ST^2 = Theta~(n). Because that bound is TIGHT and proved in the generic model, it is the ideal yardstick: if secp256k1's coordinate representation is compressible in any way a generic encoding is not, a learned advice of S bits should achieve T << sqrt(n/S). Measure the empirical slope of log T vs log S and compare with -1/2.
nongeneric_structure: The advice is computed from, and the online phase queries, the EXPLICIT coordinate representation (bit patterns of x(kP), Legendre symbols, x mod small primes, lambda-orbit invariants), none of which exist for opaque encodings; the Corrigan-Gibbs/Kogan lower bound applies only to generic advice, so beating slope -1/2 is not forbidden and would be a real statement about F_p structure.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Corrigan-Gibbs & Kogan 2018 (EUROCRYPT) 'The Discrete-Logarithm Problem with Preprocessing' - generic lower bound ST^2 = Omega~(n). [ESTABLISHED] Bernstein & Lange 2013 (ASIACRYPT) 'Non-uniform cracks in the concrete: the power of free precomputation' and Bernstein & Lange (INDOCRYPT 2012) 'Computing small discrete logarithms faster' - matching algorithmic side. SEARCH: 'Mihalcik 2010 thesis discrete logarithm preprocessing time-space tradeoff' - should be the original table-based S T^2 = n algorithm. SEARCH: 'neural network discrete logarithm elliptic curve learning' - expect only negative or non-reproducible results; treat any positive claim as unverified. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: prior work compares TABLE advice against the generic bound; here the advice is a lossy model, honestly measured in bits after entropy coding, and the experiment is framed so that the comparison is apples-to-apples against a table of identical bit size.
smallest_experiment: Curves at 20, 24, 28 and 30 bits (full group tables computable). Classical arm: build a Mihalcik/Bernstein-Lange style advice of S bits (distinguished points with their logs, entropy-coded), then solve 200 random targets with a kangaroo walk that halts on a stored point; measure T in group operations using the repo's C rho core (/home/user/virtualaquarium/ecdlp/csrc/rho.c, lib/librho.so) for exact op counts. ML arm: train models with parameter budgets S in {2^8, 2^10, ..., 2^18} bits to predict the bucket index of k among 2^j buckets from features of (x,y) (raw bits, x mod small primes, Legendre symbol, symmetric functions of the lambda-orbit {x, beta x, beta^2 x}); online phase = evaluate model, run BSGS/kangaroo inside the predicted bucket, fall back to a full kangaroo on misprediction; count ALL online group operations including fallbacks, and count model evaluation cost in group-operation equivalents. Report S post-entropy-coding (this is where naive ML claims die). Plot log2 T vs log2 S per curve size, fit slope, overlay the -1/2 generic line and the classical arm.
kill_criteria: DEAD if the fitted slope is >= -0.55 (i.e. indistinguishable from or worse than generic) at every curve size AND the ML arm never beats the classical table arm at equal honest S. DEAD also if any apparent advantage vanishes when (i) S is measured after entropy coding, (ii) the base point is changed, or (iii) the curve size increases - i.e. the model was memorising the table. An advantage that scales in b is the only survivable outcome.
expected_complexity: Slope -1 (T = n/S) would be a genuine refutation of a non-generic extension of the CGK bound, yet still gives T = 2^80 only at S = 2^176 - so be explicit: even a positive result here almost certainly does not break secp256k1; it would be evidence that coordinate structure is compressible, which then has to be turned into an attack by other means. What must be true for any asymptotic win: the map k -> representation(kP) must admit a description shorter than a table for the buckets being predicted, i.e. it must have nontrivial circuit-level or Kolmogorov structure in the k-direction.
novelty_note: Most 'ML for DLP' work has no baseline and so produces uninterpretable results; here the baseline is a tight, proved generic trade-off, which makes both outcomes meaningful - a null is a quantitative statement that coordinate representations are incompressible in the preprocessing sense, and a positive is a refutation of the natural non-generic extension of Corrigan-Gibbs/Kogan.

title: Leakage frontier: the largest number of unknown scalar bits at which a bit-level solver beats kangaroo
surface: 7a, reframed - measure the SCALING of solver leverage instead of asking whether SAT solves the full instance
hypothesis: Fix a b-bit curve and reveal all but u bits of k. Kangaroo/BSGS costs ~2*2^(u/2) group operations; a bit-level solver costs C(u,b). Define u*(b) as the largest u where the solver wins after normalising both to group-operation equivalents. If u*(b)/b trends upward with b, the solver's non-generic leverage scales and extrapolation to 256 bits is meaningful; if u*(b) saturates (expected, around 20-30 bits), the whole SAT surface is calibrated as dead with a number attached.
nongeneric_structure: Same as the scaling-law idea - the solver reasons about the F_p multiplication and pseudo-Mersenne reduction circuit - but here the baseline is the partial-information setting, where non-generic methods (lattice/HNP) are known to beat generic search, so the comparison is meaningful rather than hopeless by construction. The measurement isolates how much of that known non-generic leverage CDCL can actually reach.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Pollard kangaroo/lambda for intervals, cost ~2*sqrt(interval). [ESTABLISHED] Boneh & Venkatesan 1996 (CRYPTO) hidden number problem - lattice methods exploit leaked bits non-generically. SEARCH: 'Howgrave-Graham Smart lattice attacks on digital signature schemes 2001' - should give the standard single/multi-signature lattice thresholds. SEARCH: 'Bleichenbacher bias attack DSA nonce' - Fourier-based partial-information attack, relevant as the third baseline. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: prior work reports lattice thresholds for HNP with many samples; this measures a head-to-head, ops-normalised crossover u*(b) for a SINGLE instance against kangaroo, as a function of curve size, which is the only quantity that decides whether the SAT surface has any asymptotic content.
smallest_experiment: Reuse the encoding validated this session (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-virtualaquarium/e2bf485c-5536-57b5-8ef5-8e69bb3bcc7b/scratchpad/satpilot.py), which already recovers k correctly at 8 bits (52-68 s) and times out at 10 bits (304 s). Fix the top b-u bits of k to their true values as unit clauses; sweep u = 4,6,8,... at b in {16, 20, 24, 28, 32}; 20 random targets per cell; record median solve time and median conflicts. Measure one group operation's wall time in the SAME harness (the repo's C rho core gives ~10^7-10^8 ops/s) to convert solver time into group-operation equivalents; compare against 2*2^(u/2). Report u*(b) and fit u*(b) vs b. Ablate: unknown bits contiguous at the top vs bottom vs scattered (the pseudo-Mersenne wrap predicts low bits should be structurally different from high bits if the solver exploits reduction at all - a sharp, falsifiable sub-prediction); also add a lattice/HNP arm as a third baseline.
kill_criteria: DEAD if u*(b) is constant or decreasing in b, or if u* < 24 for all tested b - then the solver is strictly a small-interval tool and has no asymptotic content. DEAD also if the contiguous-low-bits vs contiguous-high-bits ablation shows no difference, since that means the solver is not exploiting the reduction structure at all and the special prime is irrelevant. Survives only if u*(b)/b increases measurably over b in [16,32] with non-overlapping CIs at the endpoints.
expected_complexity: For a full break one needs u*(b) >= b, i.e. u*/b -> 1. A measured u*/b of, say, 0.3 means the solver only helps when 70% of the scalar leaks - useful for side-channel work, worthless against the ECDLP itself. The precondition for any asymptotic claim: the growth of u* must be superlinear-ish in the accessible range AND the per-conflict constant must stay within ~2^20 of a group operation, which the 8-bit pilot (about 10^7x penalty) already makes look implausible.
novelty_note: Turns the 'expected answer: exponential with bad constants' into a two-parameter measurement (exponent AND crossover as a function of leakage) whose ablation on bit position is a direct, falsifiable test of whether CDCL exploits the pseudo-Mersenne prime at all - a question the raw scaling law alone cannot answer, and one that no published SAT-vs-ECDLP result addresses.

title: Quasi-homomorphism into F_p^* log-coordinates (the free subexponential-oracle bridge)
surface: 8(b) free partial information from the representation + 8(d) interaction with the multiplicative group of F_p
hypothesis: Because DLP in F_p^* is subexponential and p = X^8 - X - 977 (X = 2^32) is SNFS-special, the map L = log_g(x(.)) : E(F_p)\{O} -> Z/(p-1) is a FREE oracle for the attacker; the hypothesis is that some coordinate-built F into Z/(p-1) has an additive defect delta(P,Q) = F(P+Q)-F(P)-F(Q) that is NOT uniform - supported on n^{o(1)} values or computable from the representation - which would transfer ECDLP into a group where DL is easy.
nongeneric_structure: The x-coordinate is an element of F_p^*, whose DL is subexponential (routine at 256 bits, and cheaper still by SNFS because p is a degree-8 polynomial in 2^32); plus the EXACT relation L([lambda]P) = L(P) + log_g(beta), and the curve relation 3L(x) = log(y^2-7). A generic algorithm cannot evaluate L at all - it only sees opaque encodings - so this is not a re-encoded generic search: it consumes an oracle the generic model forbids.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Transfers that work all use HOMOMORPHISMS: MOV (Menezes-Okamoto-Vanstone 1993) and Frey-Ruck (1994) into F_{p^k}^*, dead here because the embedding degree is ~n; Smart 1999 / Satoh-Araki 1998 / Semaev 1998 into (Z/p,+), dead because n != p. [ESTABLISHED] No nontrivial homomorphism E(F_p) -> Z/(p-1) exists (n is prime and n does not divide p-1), so only quasi-homomorphisms are possible. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: the literature only ever asks for exact homomorphisms; I ask for a defect of low entropy, and I exploit the 2^128-vs-routine asymmetry between ECDLP and the field DL, which I have not seen used as an attack resource. SEARCH: 'elliptic curve discrete logarithm attack using discrete logarithm in the base field F_p' - expect the result to be that no such attack is known, only pairing transfers.
smallest_experiment: Generate toy curves y^2=x^3+7 over 20-32 bit primes p = 1 mod 3 with prime group order AND p-1 smooth (so Pohlig-Hellman logs in F_p^* are instant); reuse /home/user/virtualaquarium/ecdlp/tools/gen_curves.gp with an added smoothness filter. Build the full log table for F_p^*. For a library of candidates F in {L(x), L(y), L(x-x0), L(x^3-8b), L(x)+cL(y), L of the canonical-lift digit}, sample 10^6 random pairs (P,Q), histogram delta(P,Q), and measure its Shannon entropy and its conditional entropy given cheap side data (x mod small primes, characters). Control: replace x by a fixed random bijection E->F_p and repeat, to calibrate the finite-sample entropy bias.
kill_criteria: DEAD if for every candidate F the empirical defect entropy is within the control's 3-sigma band of log2(p-1) and the conditional entropy given cheap data drops by less than 0.05 bits, at 20, 24, 28 and 32 bits with no improving trend. Also DEAD if a defect with small support is found but computing it is shown to require the DL itself (check by trying to predict delta from (x(P),x(Q)) with a low-degree rational interpolation and falsifying on fresh pairs).
expected_complexity: If a defect supported on s values (or computable from the representation) exists: ECDLP in O(s) * (cost of field DL) + polylog, i.e. a break if s = n^{o(1)}. This requires the defect to be both low-entropy AND computable without knowing the discrete logs - both are directly measured.
novelty_note: The textbook dead end is 'no homomorphism to F_p^* exists'. This is not that statement: it accepts the non-existence of a homomorphism and asks the strictly weaker, measurable question of whether the defect cocycle is degenerate, using an oracle (field DL, made even cheaper by the SNFS shape of secp256k1's p) that no generic-group argument can account for.

title: ECDLP as a hidden-shift problem: linear Fourier is dead by Weil II, quadratic phase is not
surface: 8(a) statistical structure of k -> x(kP) + 8(f) classical analogue of period finding + 8(b)
hypothesis: With f(j) = chi(x(jP)) for an algebraic character chi of F_p, ECDLP is exactly a hidden-shift problem: we can evaluate f anywhere, and evaluate f_k(j) = f(k+j) anywhere from Q = kP. Deligne's bound makes all LINEAR Fourier coefficients O(n^{-1/2}) so no U^2 attack exists; but nothing bounds the correlation of f with a QUADRATIC phase e_n(ak^2+bk), which is precisely what elliptic-divisibility-sequence / theta / canonical-height structure would produce. If that correlation is delta >= n^{-eps}, list-decoding recovers k in poly(1/delta).
nongeneric_structure: chi(x(.)) is an algebraic function of the coordinate representation, with the exact CM equivariance f(lambda*j) = omega * f(j) for the cubic character (verified-relevant: 3 exactly divides p-1 for secp256k1, so chi_3(beta) != 1). Quadratic phases would come from the EDS relation x(kP) = x(P) - W_{k-1}W_{k+1}/W_k^2 and the quadratic growth of the canonical height. A generic algorithm sees a uniformly random f, whose U^3 norm is exactly the random baseline; any excess is non-generic by definition.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Kohel-Shparlinski (ANTS 2000, 'Exponential sums and group generators for elliptic curves over finite fields') and related Shparlinski work bound linear exponential sums over E, i.e. exactly the U^2 quantity; Deligne's Weil II gives |sum_j psi(j)chi(x(jP))| = O(sqrt n) because such a character of E(F_p) is a Lang-torsor rank-1 sheaf. [ESTABLISHED] Akavia-Goldwasser-Safra (FOCS 2003, 'Proving hard-core predicates using list decoding') recovers a hidden shift in time poly(1/delta) from a concentrated Fourier spectrum with query access - and we HAVE query access. [ESTABLISHED] Green-Tao inverse theorem for the U^3 norm. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: the standard pseudorandomness results are strictly about linear sums; completing a quadratic phase into linear characters loses a factor sqrt(n) and gives only the trivial bound, so the U^3 question is genuinely uncontrolled by the published bounds.
smallest_experiment: Toy curves with 2^20 <= n <= 2^26 (numpy FFT is fine to 2^26 in float32). For chi in {Legendre, cubic, sextic character of x; MSB of x; parity of popcount}: (1) exact max Fourier coefficient by FFT (expect the Weil baseline ~ sqrt(log n / n)); (2) the U^3 norm estimated by sampling the double derivative, and more sharply: for each of 10^3 random shifts h, FFT the derivative Delta_h f(j) = f(j+h) conj(f(j)) and record its largest coefficient - a quadratic phase makes Delta_h f a LINEAR phase of slope 2ah, so the heavy coefficient must appear at a frequency linear in h. Control: an i.i.d. random sign sequence of the same length, plus a planted quadratic phase at known delta to calibrate detection power.
kill_criteria: DEAD if, for every chi, max_h (largest Fourier coefficient of Delta_h f) lies inside the control's empirical 99.9th percentile at n = 2^20, 2^22, 2^24, 2^26 AND shows no growth relative to the sqrt(log n/n) baseline, while the planted-signal calibration shows the test would have detected delta >= n^{-0.2}.
expected_complexity: poly(1/delta) group operations if the U^3 correlation is delta; a break needs delta >= n^{-eps} with eps < 1/4 for the naive sampling version, or any inverse-polynomial delta for the AGS/derivative version. Must be true: the concentration must be at frequencies findable by query access, not merely existent.
novelty_note: Everyone cites 'x(kP) is pseudorandom' and stops; the cited theorems only cover degree-1 (linear) structure. Testing degree-2 structure, with a named mechanism (EDS/canonical height quadratic growth) for why degree 2 and not degree 1 is where it could hide, and with a concrete list-decoding payoff, is not a restatement of the linear dead end.

title: Free extra p-adic digits: the canonical lift, the multiplicative second digit, and the unique defect function b
surface: 8(b) free partial information + lifting to characteristic 0 done the one way that is actually computable
hypothesis: E(F_p) embeds by a CHEAP computable group isomorphism into E~(Z/p^m), where E~: y^2=x^3+7 over Z_p is the Serre-Tate canonical lift; so every point carries m*256 free bits. Define h(P) in F_p by x(P~) = omega(x_P)(1 + p*h(P)) with omega the Teichmuller lift. Hypothesis: some function of the extra digits is additive up to a defect that is a LOW-DEGREE RATIONAL FUNCTION of the coordinates - which would be a break, because the unique b with coboundary equal to that defect is exactly the missing homomorphism.
nongeneric_structure: j=0 with CM by the maximal order Z[omega] and class number 1, so the canonical lift is the reduction-of-a-global-curve y^2=x^3+7 itself (Deuring lifting); E(F_p) = ker(pi~ - 1) which is n-torsion on the lift. I VERIFIED the computable lift on a 20-bit toy curve (/tmp/.../scratchpad/lift.py): P~ = [p^{-m} mod n]([p^m](Hensel lift of P)) is a group homomorphism, n-torsion mod p^2, and lambda acts as x -> Teichmuller(beta)*x. Generic groups have no digits at all, so this is the opposite of a re-encoded generic search.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Smart 1999 / Satoh-Araki 1998 / Semaev 1998: the lift-and-take-formal-logarithm attack works exactly when n = p, and for n != p it fails for a NAMEABLE reason: the lifted point is n-torsion, so its formal/elliptic logarithm is identically zero. [ESTABLISHED] Satoh 2000 canonical-lift point counting supplies the lifting machinery. [ESTABLISHED] Serre-Tate theory: the canonical lift is precisely the deformation with trivial Serre-Tate parameter, so the Serre-Tate pairing gives nothing on it - which is why I also propose NON-canonical lifts, where the defect is a genuine nonzero symmetric 2-cocycle c(P,Q) with values in the formal group (=F_p at level p^2). [ESTABLISHED] H^2(Z/n, F_p) = 0 since gcd(n,p)=1, so c = coboundary of a UNIQUE function b, and ECDLP is equivalent to computing b faster than n steps.
smallest_experiment: Toy curves 20-28 bits. (1) Compute h(P) for all P (cheap: one Hensel lift, one [p] and one scalar mult per point mod p^2) and measure the entropy of the additivity defect of h against a control. (2) The decisive test: for a non-canonical lift (e.g. naive integer lift of x), compute the cocycle c explicitly, compute b by the O(n) averaging formula b(P) = (1/n) sum_Q c(P,Q) on a curve with n ~ 2^22, then test whether b(P) is a rational function of x(P) of degree <= D: interpolate on D+2 points via Cauchy/Pade (numpy or sympy over F_p) for D = 1..1000 and FALSIFY on fresh points. (3) Repeat with b restricted to a lambda-orbit transversal.
kill_criteria: DEAD if b is not a rational function of x of degree <= 1000 at n ~ 2^22 (interpolation always falsifies on fresh points), AND the defect entropy of h matches the control at all sizes, AND the same holds when b is replaced by its composition with the field log. A positive result is unmistakable: an interpolated b that predicts fresh points is an immediate break.
expected_complexity: If b is a rational function of degree D in x, ECDLP costs O~(D) field operations, i.e. a full break for D = polylog. This requires the canonical defect function to be algebraic of low degree - a strong requirement, but one that is cheaply falsifiable and has never, to my knowledge, been measured.
novelty_note: The known dead end is 'lift and take the formal logarithm - it vanishes'. I am not taking a logarithm: I am using the cohomological fact that the missing homomorphism's defect is a computable coboundary with a UNIQUE primitive b, and testing whether b is algebraic. The computable canonical lift (verified above) also hands the attacker extra digits nobody has audited.

title: ECDLP as an Artin symbol: explicit class field theory of Q(omega) and elliptic units
surface: 8-wildcard: the CM / char-0 arithmetic of the one global curve secp256k1 reduces from
hypothesis: secp256k1 is the reduction of the single global CM curve y^2=x^3+7 over K=Q(omega), and E(F_p) is the n-torsion group ker(pi~-1) on it. Because of CM, K(x(E[n])) is ABELIAN over K with Galois group (Z[omega]/(pi-1))^* modulo units, acting on the points BY SCALARS - so the discrete log IS an Artin symbol. Hypothesis: a Galois-equivariant invariant (an elliptic/Siegel unit at the torsion point) can be computed p-adically from the coordinates and descended, by a norm to a degree-d subfield, to something matching a table of size d - yielding k's coset modulo an index-d subgroup of (Z/n)^*, which is worth sqrt(n/d) by the reduction in idea multiplicative-coset-leak.
nongeneric_structure: Abelian division fields with scalar Galois action. This is the sharpest non-generic property available: for a non-CM curve the n-division field has Galois group GL_2(Z/n) and no such structure exists. The generic model has no Galois theory at all, so this cannot be a re-encoded generic search.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] CM theory: Deuring lifting, Shimura reciprocity, ray class fields of K generated by Weber-function values at torsion (Lang, 'Elliptic Functions', ch. 10). [ESTABLISHED] Elliptic units and their distribution relations: Kubert-Lang 'Modular Units' (1981), Coates-Wiles (1977), Robert. [ESTABLISHED] The nearest cryptanalytic relative, Silverman's xedni calculus (1998) and its refutation by Jacobson-Koblitz-Silverman-Stengle-Teske (2000), failed because lifting a RANDOM point to a global point forces astronomically large height. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: I never lift a random point - the points are already torsion on a fixed global curve, their field is abelian, and elliptic units are the objects whose heights are governed by the Kronecker limit formula / Stark regulators rather than by naive lifting. THE BLOCKERS I must name honestly: (i) reconstructing an algebraic number from p-adic data needs precision proportional to its height, which for degree-n torsion data is exponential; (ii) taking a norm needs the Galois conjugates, which needs the DL - circular unless a distribution relation or a p-adic L-value supplies the norm for free. SEARCH: 'elliptic units attack discrete logarithm CM elliptic curve' and 'p-adic L-function Katz measure elliptic unit computable exponential sum' - expect: no such attack in the literature, and Katz's p-adic L-functions do give poly-time evaluation of certain exponentially long sums of elliptic-unit logarithms.
smallest_experiment: PARI-GP, toy sizes only. (1) Sanity: for tiny n (7, 13, 19, 31) verify with nfisincl/factorization of the n-division polynomial over Q(omega) that the x-coordinate field is abelian of degree (n-1)/6 - confirms the scalar Galois action concretely. (2) Reconstruction-cost law: on 20-24 bit toy curves take a torsion point of the global curve, compute a Siegel/elliptic-unit value p-adically to precision p^m (Newton/Hensel on the sigma or theta expansion), and measure the smallest m for which LLL recognizes it as an algebraic number of degree d, for d = 2..16; fit m vs n across several curves. (3) Test whether any distribution relation gives a norm down a Galois subgroup (rather than down conductor) without conjugates.
kill_criteria: DEAD if the fitted exponent of m against n is >= 0.9 (precision grows essentially linearly in n, so reconstruction is exponential), AND no distribution relation produces a norm to an index-d subfield without explicit conjugates. Either half alone kills the reconstruction route.
expected_complexity: If a free norm to a degree-d subfield existed with poly-size p-adic reconstruction, one gets k's coset mod an index-d subgroup and hence sqrt(n/d) group operations; a break needs d = n^{eps}, which for secp256k1's n-1 = 2^6*3*149*631*(232-bit cofactor) means the 232-bit cofactor would have to be factorable into usable pieces too.
novelty_note: I have not seen the cryptanalytic statement 'for a CM curve the ECDLP is literally the evaluation of an Artin symbol in an abelian extension' used as an attack plan, nor the idea of descending elliptic-unit data to small subfields to leak a multiplicative coset. It is strange, but every step is a standard theorem, and the two blockers are stated in advance as the kill criteria.

title: Beating birthday needs a hash that detects a whole difference set, not just equality
surface: 8(h) coordinate LSH + 8(g) non-generic rho
hypothesis: Rho and BSGS cost sqrt(n) because only the event P-Q = 0 (or P-Q in an Aut-orbit, |T| = 6) is detectable by hashing. If a coordinate-derived hash h makes the event P-Q in T detectable for a set T with |T| = n^delta - i.e. Pr[h(P)=h(Q) | P-Q in T] exceeds the random collision rate by a factor ~|T| - then the walk needs only sqrt(n/|T|) steps and the whole problem drops to n^{(1-delta)/2}.
nongeneric_structure: The hash reads the coordinate representation. In the generic model the conditional and unconditional collision rates are provably equal, so a measured excess is by itself a refutation of genericity for this curve; nothing here can be re-encoded as a generic search.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Wiener-Zuccherato (1998) and Gallant-Lambert-Vanstone (2000) achieve exactly the |T| = 6 case using automorphism classes, the only known instance; Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe (2011) on the negation map handles the fruitless-cycle bookkeeping. [ESTABLISHED, in this repo] null_battery.py group C tested translation-distortion of coordinate metrics and null_battery2.py corrected its statistics - both null. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: group C asked whether a metric is approximately translation-invariant; the cost formula does not actually need a metric, it needs a conditional collision ratio for a FIXED KNOWN difference set, which is a different (and strictly weaker) requirement, and I include hash families that are not metrics at all: canonical-lift digits, Lattes-orbit minima, and character vectors. [ESTABLISHED] A rigorous partial no-go worth recording: any hash whose level sets are unions of cosets is impossible for prime n, so only non-invariant hashes are in play.
smallest_experiment: 24-32 bit curves, C rho harness already in /home/user/virtualaquarium/ecdlp/csrc/rho.c for the baseline. Fix P0 and T = {+-jP0 : j <= t} for t in {2,8,64,1024}. Hash candidates: top-b bits of x; x mod each of 20 small primes; the vector of Legendre/cubic characters of x+c_i; b bits of the canonical-lift digit h(P); min over the short phi_2-orbit of x; SimHash of the bit vector of x. For 10^7 sampled pairs with P-Q in T and 10^7 uniform pairs, estimate r = Pr[collision | P-Q in T] / Pr[collision | random], with binomial error bars and a control in which x is replaced by a random bijection.
kill_criteria: DEAD (and with it the whole LSH surface) if r-1 is within 3 sigma of 0 for every hash, every t, and every curve size, while a planted-structure calibration shows the test would detect r >= 1.05. Record the best observed r as an upper bound on what any future hash of this type can buy.
expected_complexity: n^{(1-delta)/2} group operations if some hash achieves an excess ratio scaling like n^delta; needs the ratio to GROW with n, not merely exceed 1 at one size - a constant ratio is only a constant-factor gain.
novelty_note: It reframes 'LSH for ECDLP' into the exact quantity that appears in the cost formula - a conditional collision ratio for a known difference set - which makes the surface decisively falsifiable rather than vaguely hopeless, and it tests hash families (p-adic digits, Lattes orbits) that the existing null battery did not contain.

title: A multiplicative character of k would buy sqrt(n/d): audit every free predicate, and validate the payoff
surface: 8(b) free partial information + 8(e) Cheon-style auxiliary data
hypothesis: The hard world Z/n is sandwiched between two EASY worlds: F_p^* and (Z/n)^*, both with subexponential DL. If the coset of k in an index-d subgroup of (Z/n)^* were learnable from the representation, then writing k = c*g^i with ord_n(g) = (n-1)/d turns ECDLP into a BSGS over i in the free transitive action R -> [g]R, costing sqrt(n/d)*log n group operations. For secp256k1 the freely available d from n-1 = 2^6*3*149*631*(232-bit cofactor) is about 2^24, i.e. 2^116 if any such leak existed.
nongeneric_structure: DL in (Z/n)^* (n prime, 256 bits) is routine, and the question is whether the COORDINATES leak a multiplicative character of k. Also included is a rigorous no-go that is itself non-generic: every morphism E -> E is [alpha] + T, so all data freely derivable from Q by morphisms has discrete log AFFINE in k; Cheon's [k^d]P is therefore provably not free, and the only free non-morphism data is coordinate feedback k -> lift(x(kP)) mod n, which is exactly what rho already consumes.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Cheon (EUROCRYPT 2006, 'Security analysis of the strong Diffie-Hellman problem') achieves sqrt(n/d) for d dividing n+-1 given auxiliary powers - the same sqrt(n/d) shape, obtained from multiplicative structure on the exponent, which is why the payoff side of this idea is credible. [ESTABLISHED] Boneh-Shparlinski (CRYPTO 2001, 'On the unpredictability of bits of the elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman scheme') and the hard-core-bit literature predict the leak is null. [ESTABLISHED] Damgard (1988) on Legendre sequences and Russell-Shparlinski (2004, 'Classical and quantum function reconstruction via character evaluation') on the shifted-character problem: note we could evaluate chi(k+j) for all j from Q+jP if any single-character leak existed. WHAT IS DIFFERENT from the repo's existing null battery A: that battery tested k's BITS and residues modulo small integers; a multiplicative character chi_q(k) modulo the 256-bit prime n is not a function of any of those features and was never tested.
smallest_experiment: Two halves, both cheap. (A) Leak audit: generate toy curves where n-1 has a prime factor q in {3,...,1000} (filter in gen_curves.gp); for all k compute chi_q(k) = k^{(n-1)/q} mod n and test dependence on coordinate features (bits of x, x mod small primes, Legendre/cubic characters of x, the canonical-lift digit h, the field log L(x)) with chi^2 and mutual-information estimates, calibrated against a control where kP is replaced by a random bijection. (B) Payoff validation, independent of (A): on a 40-bit curve, GRANT the oracle chi_q(k) for q | n-1, implement the coset BSGS over the action R -> [g]R, and verify empirically that the cost really is sqrt(n/d)*log n.
kill_criteria: Leak DEAD if the estimated mutual information between every feature and chi_q(k) stays below 10^-3 bits with control-calibrated thresholds at 24, 28, 32 bits with no trend. The payoff half is DEAD only if the granted-oracle BSGS fails to hit sqrt(n/d) - in which case the reduction itself was wrong and should be discarded.
expected_complexity: sqrt(n/d)*log n group operations given a coset leak at index d; a genuine asymptotic win needs d = n^{eps}, which for secp256k1 additionally needs usable factors of the 232-bit cofactor of n-1. What must be true: a computable predicate on the representation correlated with a multiplicative character of k.
novelty_note: The two-easy-worlds framing (F_p^* below, (Z/n)^* above, hard Z/n between) plus the concrete observation that a multiplicative coset of k is worth sqrt(n/d) by plain BSGS in the g-action is, as far as I know, unwritten; the accompanying morphism no-go turns the vague 'Cheon needs unavailable data' into a proof about what is and is not free.

title: Functional-graph anomalies of Lattes walks on the Kummer line
surface: 8(c) Lattes / arithmetic dynamics + 8(g) non-generic rho walk
hypothesis: On E/{+-1} = P^1 the multiplication maps are Lattes maps phi_m, and for gcd(m, n * n_twist) = 1 they are PERMUTATIONS with algebraically forced cycle length ord(m), i.e. maximally non-random compared to the Flajolet-Odlyzko random-map baseline. Hypothesis: a rho walk mixing cheap Lattes steps with additive steps has functional-graph statistics (cyclic-node count, component count, expected rho length) that deviate from the random-map prediction; a deviation scaling like n^{1/2-eps} would break the birthday bound.
nongeneric_structure: phi_m is a rational map on the coordinate line, computed with x-only arithmetic (doubling is ~5 field multiplications versus ~11 for a full addition), the lambda map is a SINGLE field multiplication, and the walk's cycle structure is governed by multiplicative orders mod n - a quantity invisible to a generic algorithm, which sees only an abstract group with no maps but translations.
prior_work: [ESTABLISHED] Flajolet-Odlyzko (1990) random-mapping statistics give the baseline sqrt(pi n / 2) cyclic nodes. [ESTABLISHED] Teske (2001, 'On random walks for Pollard's rho method') measured collision performance of additive walks and found r-adding walks near-random; Bernstein-Lange-Schwabe (2011) handled negation-map cycles. [ESTABLISHED] Vasiga-Shallit (2004) showed functional graphs of x^2 and x^2-2 over F_p are completely non-random, determined by multiplicative orders. SEARCH: 'Ugolini functional graph Lattes maps elliptic curves finite fields' - expect a result describing the cycle structure of phi_m on P^1(F_p) purely in terms of ord(m) mod n and mod the twist order. WHAT IS DIFFERENT: prior EC-rho work measured only additive walks; nobody has measured whether MIXING algebraically-structured permutations with additive steps biases the collision time, and the known extreme non-randomness of the pure Lattes graph is at least a reason to look.
smallest_experiment: 20-26 bit curves, exhaustive enumeration. Build the mixed walk W(x) = one of {phi_2(x), phi_3(x), x-coordinate of (P_x + R_i)} selected by a hash of x, as an explicit array of size ~n/2 on the Kummer line; count cyclic nodes, tails, components exactly; compare against the random-map prediction and against a control walk on an abstract cyclic group of the same order. Separately measure the mean rho length over 10^4 random starts and compare with sqrt(pi n / 4) for the +-quotient. Instrument the existing C rho in csrc/rho.c for a fair operations-per-second comparison so the cheap-step constant factor is measured separately from the step count.
kill_criteria: DEAD (asymptotically) if cyclic-node count, component count and mean rho length all lie within 2% of the random-map predictions at 20, 22, 24 and 26 bits with no trend in the residual. Note that even then the x-only step cost may give a constant-factor engineering gain, which must be reported as such and NOT as a complexity win.
expected_complexity: n^{1/2-eps} only if the cyclic-node count scales below sqrt(n); anything else is at best a constant factor. What must be true: the algebraic constraint on cycle lengths must survive the mixing with additive steps, which is exactly what the measurement checks.
novelty_note: The specific claim being tested - that composing algebraically forced permutations (Lattes maps, whose cycle lengths are multiplicative orders) with additive steps might bias collision statistics - is not the usual 'rho walks are heuristically random' assertion; it is the one place where the Kummer-line dynamics impose a hard algebraic constraint on the walk's graph, and it is exhaustively checkable at toy sizes.
